that care in fact-finding would be a priority concern in all of these 
rulemaking contexts; what is not easy to spot is how these rulemaking 
contexts differ in that regard from rulemaking under any number of other 
statutes enacted during the 1970s or during any other decade.
A series of judicial ruhngs in the 1970s imposed similar obligations 
without explicit legislative sanction. The D.C. and the Fourth Circuits 
purported to require agencies making rules based on the resolution of 
complex technical issues to provide participants at least limited trial-type 
procedures. See, e,g., Int'l Harvester Co, v, Ruckelshaus, 478 F.2d 615 (D.C. 
Cir. 1973); Appalachian Power Co. v, EPA, 477 F.2d 495 (4th Cir. 1973); 
Walter Holm & Co. v. Hardin, 449 F.2d 1009 (D.C. Cir. 1971).
Mobil Oil Corp. v. Federal Power Commission, 483 F.2d 1238 (D.C. Cir. 
1973), for example, was a suit to review a Federal Power Commission (FPC) 
order setting minimum rates charged by natural gas pipelines for 
transporting liquid hydrocarbons. The petitioners raised a host of 
objections to the FPC’s order, among them the claim that the agency had 
improperly denied them the opportunity to cross-examine the evidence on 
which it rehed in allocating pipeline costs between gaseous and hquid 
products. Though the Natural Gas Act specified that it could act only “after 
a hearing,” the FPC contended that, under Florida East Coast, it need only 
comply with section 553.
While Judge Wilkey, writing for the court, agreed that the FPC was 
not statutorily required to engage in formal rulemaking, he held the agency 
was still obhgated to accord the petitioners a broader opportunity to contest 
its factual premises than traditional informal procedures could assure:
The Natural Gas Act exphcitly states that factual 
determinations must be supported by “substantial evidence.” 
Unlike many other forms of rulemaking, rate-making necessarily 
rests upon findings of facts.
* * * Clearly some evidence supporting the FPC’s finding 
must be in the record. More importantly for our purposes, the rule 
that the ''whole record'' be considered—both evidence for and 
against—means that the procedures must provide some 
mechanism for interested parties to introduce adverse evidence and 
criticize evidence introduced by others. This process of 
introduction and criticism helps assure that the factual basis of 
the FPC rates will be accurate and provides the reviewing court 
with a record from which it can determine if the agency has 
properly exercised its discretion. * * *
Informal comments simply cannot create a record that 
satisfies the substantial evidence test. Even if controverting
